  pagetitle: "Regime-Dependent Allocation"
  description-meta: "Regime-switching asset allocation in R: the Hamilton filter and a two-state hidden Markov model written inline, a turbulence threshold, regime.portfolios() in PortfolioAnalytics, and an out-of-sample test of detected against dated regimes."
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/_common.R")
library(tidypm)
library(knitr)
```

What if the right portfolio depends on the state of the world? @hamilton1989
gave that question its statistical form, a series whose parameters switch with
an unobserved Markov chain, and @ang2002a carried the form into portfolio
choice, with an international investor who faces a normal regime and a bear
regime of lower means, higher volatilities and higher correlations. The
descriptive chapters supplied the reason to ask. In
@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application the tails of this market arrived as a
handful of episodes in which correlations rose, and in
@sec-14-risk-based-allocation-application the effective number of bets fell in
the same months.

This is a **tactical** chapter in the sense of
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory: the allocation is conditioned on a
state inferred at the time, and deviates from a policy estimated without one.
We first state the regime-switching model, the filter that infers its state
and the mixture moments an investor faces one month ahead; then date the
regimes of the modeled market with hindsight, detect them without it in two
ways, a turbulence threshold and a two-state hidden Markov model, and show what
`PortfolioAnalytics` offers for switching between portfolio specifications; and
finally ask whether a regime-switching allocation is ahead of a static one out
of sample once the regime has to be detected rather than dated.

The data are the sixteen risky class series of
@sec-02-notation-and-data-simulated-market, in excess of the Treasury bill for
the reasons of @sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory.

```{r}
#| label: data
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)   # sixteen risky classes
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return                                  # the bill
Re <- R - rf                                                       # excess returns
N  <- ncol(Re); dates <- zoo::index(R); X <- zoo::coredata(Re)
ep <- sim_episodes                                                 # the four named episodes
stopifnot(N == 16L, !anyNA(Re), all(sim_riskfree_monthly$date == dates))
```

## Regimes, Filters, and Mixtures {#sec-19-regimes-theory}

### The regime-switching model

Let $s_t \in \{1, \dots, K\}$ be an unobserved state and $\boldsymbol{r}_t$ the
vector of excess returns. In the model of @hamilton1989, applied to returns,

$$
\boldsymbol{r}_t \mid s_t = s \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_s, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_s),
\qquad
\Pr(s_{t+1} = j \mid s_t = i) = p_{ij},
$$ {#eq-19-model}

with the $p_{ij}$ collected in a transition matrix $\boldsymbol{P}$ whose rows
sum to one. A regime lasts $1/(1 - p_{ss})$ periods on average, and the chain
spends a long-run share $\bar{\pi}_s$ of its time in state $s$, where
$\bar{\boldsymbol{\pi}}'\boldsymbol{P} = \bar{\boldsymbol{\pi}}'$. @turner1989
fitted a two-state version to excess stock returns, with a mean and a variance
that both switch, and @ang2012 survey what the model has been used for since.

### The Hamilton filter

The state is never observed, so everything rests on the probability of each
state given the returns seen so far. Write $\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|\tau}$ for the
vector with elements $\Pr(s_t = j \mid \boldsymbol{r}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{r}_\tau)$
and $\boldsymbol{\eta}_t$ for the vector of regime densities
$f(\boldsymbol{r}_t \mid s_t = j)$. The filter of @hamilton1989 alternates two
steps. The prediction step moves the probabilities one period through the
chain,

$$
\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t+1|t} = \boldsymbol{P}'\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|t},
$$ {#eq-19-predict}

and the update step reweights them by how well each regime explains the new
observation,

$$
\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|t}
= \frac{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|t-1} \odot \boldsymbol{\eta}_t}
       {\boldsymbol{\iota}'\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|t-1} \odot \boldsymbol{\eta}_t\right)},
$$ {#eq-19-update}

where $\odot$ is the elementwise product. The denominator is the density of
$\boldsymbol{r}_t$ given the past, so the sum of its logarithms is the
log-likelihood. It is maximized by the EM algorithm of @dempster1977, which for
a hidden Markov chain is the procedure of @baum1970 and was adapted to
regime-switching models by @hamilton1990: given state probabilities, the means,
variances and transition frequencies are weighted sample moments; given those,
the probabilities are recomputed.

The probabilities EM needs use the whole sample. They are the **smoothed**
probabilities $\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|T}$, obtained from the **filtered** ones by
the backward recursion of @kim1994,

$$
\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|T}
= \boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|t} \odot
  \left[\boldsymbol{P}\left(\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t+1|T} \oslash \boldsymbol{\xi}_{t+1|t}\right)\right],
$$ {#eq-19-smooth}

with $\oslash$ elementwise division. The difference between
$\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|t}$ and $\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t|T}$ is the subject of this
chapter.

### One-step-ahead moments as a mixture

An investor standing at $t$ does not know $s_{t+1}$. With
$\boldsymbol{\pi} = \boldsymbol{\xi}_{t+1|t}$, next month's return is a mixture
of the regime distributions, with mean and covariance

$$
\bar{\boldsymbol{\mu}} = \sum_{s} \pi_s \boldsymbol{\mu}_s,
\qquad
\bar{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \sum_{s} \pi_s \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_s
  + \sum_{s} \pi_s \left(\boldsymbol{\mu}_s - \bar{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\right)
                   \left(\boldsymbol{\mu}_s - \bar{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\right)'.
$$ {#eq-19-mixture}

The covariance is not the average of the regime covariances. The second sum,
the between-regime term, is the risk of not knowing which regime next month
belongs to, and it is largest for the assets whose means differ most across
regimes. A mixture of normals is also not normal. For a single series whose
regimes share a mean, the variance is $\bar{\sigma}^2 = \sum_s \pi_s \sigma_s^2$
and the excess kurtosis is

$$
\bar{K} = 3\left(\frac{\sum_s \pi_s \sigma_s^4}{\left(\sum_s \pi_s \sigma_s^2\right)^2} - 1\right) \;\geq\; 0,
$$ {#eq-19-kurtosis}

strictly positive whenever the regime variances differ, and skewness appears as
soon as the low-mean regime is also the high-variance one [@timmermann2000].
Regimes therefore produce the fat tails and the asymmetry of
@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application from Gaussian ingredients, which
@ryden1998 found sufficient for most stylized facts of daily returns. They
produce them jointly, because all assets change regime together: the
co-moments that @sec-11-higher-moments-theory carries as tensors are here the
by-product of two covariance matrices, and @ang2002 find that a
regime-switching model reproduces the higher correlations of falling markets
documented by @longin2001 better than the alternatives they test.

### Two ways to use the state

Given $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ there are two rules. The first treats @eq-19-mixture
as the inputs of @sec-09-mean-variance-theory and holds the tangency portfolio
of @eq-09-tangency computed from $\bar{\boldsymbol{\mu}}$ and
$\bar{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$; its weights move continuously with the
probabilities. The second holds one of $K$ portfolios, each built for one
regime, and switches when the most probable regime changes,

$$
\boldsymbol{w}_t = \boldsymbol{w}^{(\hat{s}_{t+1})},
\qquad
\hat{s}_{t+1} = \arg\max_s \, \pi_s .
$$ {#eq-19-switch}

The two agree when one probability is one and differ in between, where the
mixture rule holds a compromise and the switching rule a bet. @clarke1998
showed for two states how a state-dependent mix enlarges the opportunity set of
a static one. @ang2002a solve the dynamic problem of an investor with constant
relative risk aversion and find the cost of ignoring regimes small for an
all-equity investor and substantial once a risk-free asset can be held, because
the bear regime is then a reason to leave the market; @ang2004 turn that into a
mean-variance rule and report that it outperforms static allocations out of
sample. @guidolin2007 need four regimes to describe stocks and bonds jointly,
@guidolin2008 add preferences over skewness and kurtosis, and @tu2010 finds
that a Bayesian investor who ignores regimes gives up more than two percent a
year in certainty-equivalent terms. The out-of-sample evidence on simple
switching rules in @bulla2011 and @nystrup2015, both of which leave equities
for safer assets on a filtered state, is favorable.

All of these condition on a state estimated from the data, and the estimate is
where the difficulty lies.

### Dating and detecting

A regime can be established in two ways that are easily confused. **Dating**
assigns each month to a regime with the whole sample in view: by a rule that
locates peaks and troughs, as in @pagan2003, by naming episodes after the fact,
or by the smoothed probabilities of @eq-19-smooth. **Detecting** assigns month
$t$ using only what was known at $t$: the filtered probabilities of
@eq-19-update, computed with parameters that were themselves estimated on data
through $t$. A turning point needs observations on both sides to be
recognized, so detection lags dating, and @chauvet2008 measure that lag for
business-cycle turning points in months.

A backtest of a regime strategy has three places to leak. Smoothed
probabilities at $t$ contain returns after $t$. Filtered probabilities computed
with full-sample parameters contain them less visibly, because the parameters
that describe the stress regime were learned from the very months the filter
then appears to recognize. And the regime definition itself, the number of
states and the series they are fitted to, is usually settled after looking at
the sample. The first two are coding errors of the kind
@sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-implementation guards against by lagging and
asserting, and we assert them away below. The third is the design problem of
@sec-25-backtesting-application and cannot be asserted away.

### Turbulence as a model-free detector

A regime model has parameters to estimate before it says anything. The
turbulence index of @eq-05-turbulence has none beyond a trailing mean and
covariance matrix: it measures how unusual this month's return vector is by
the standards of the recent past. @chow1999 used it to separate a calm from a
turbulent subsample and blended the two covariance matrices according to the
probability of, and the aversion to, each regime, which is the first sum of
@eq-19-mixture with $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ chosen by the investor. @kritzman2010
documented that turbulence is persistent and that risk is poorly rewarded
while it lasts, the two properties a detector needs, and @kritzman2012 fitted
hidden Markov models to turbulence and to macroeconomic series and reported
out-of-sample gains from tilting on the filtered state. A threshold on the
index is the simplest detector there is: stress when $d_t$ exceeds a quantile
of its own past.

## Implementation {#sec-19-regimes-implementation}

### Regimes dated with hindsight

`sim_episodes` names four stress episodes, and `in_episode()` places each month
inside or outside them. The moments of the sixteen classes in each state are
one grouped computation.

```{r}
#| label: dated
state <- rep("remaining months", nrow(Re))
for (k in ep$episode) state[in_episode(dates, k)] <- ep$label[ep$episode == k]
in_any <- state != "remaining months"
stopifnot(sum(in_any) == sum(vapply(ep$episode, function(k) sum(in_episode(dates, k)), integer(1))))

block_mean <- function(Z, suffix) 12 * mean(Z[, grepl(suffix, colnames(Z)), drop = FALSE])
dated <- lapply(c(ep$label, "remaining months"), function(s) {
  Z <- X[state == s, , drop = FALSE]; C <- stats::cor(Z)
  tibble::tibble(state = s, months = nrow(Z),
                 equity = block_mean(Z, "_equity$"), government = block_mean(Z, "_government$"),
                 credit = block_mean(Z, "_credit$"),
                 vol = mean(apply(Z, 2, stats::sd)) * sqrt(12),
                 correlation = mean(C[upper.tri(C)]))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-19-dated
#| tbl-cap: "The sixteen classes inside each dated episode and in the remaining months. Mean excess returns are annualized averages over the five equity, government and credit series; volatility is the average annualized volatility of the sixteen; correlation is their average pairwise correlation. A description with hindsight, not an estimate."
#| echo: false
dated |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(equity, government, credit, vol), ~ sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * .x)),
                vol = sub("^[+]", "", vol), correlation = sprintf("%.2f", correlation)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrrr",
        col.names = c("", "months", "equity", "government", "credit", "volatility", "correlation"))
```

```{r}
#| label: dated-facts
#| include: false
dv <- function(s, col) dated[[col]][dated$state == s]
gov_up <- sum(dated$government[dated$state != "remaining months"] > 0)
stopifnot(all(dated$equity[dated$state != "remaining months"] < 0),
          dv("rates shock", "government") < 0)
```

Equities lose in all four episodes. Government bonds gain in `r gov_up` of
them and lose `r sprintf("%.0f%%", -100 * dv("rates shock", "government"))` a
year in the fourth, the rates shock, so the four are not one stress regime
observed four times, which is the point
@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application made from cumulative returns. Average
correlation is `r sprintf("%.2f", dv("remaining months", "correlation"))` in
the remaining months and between
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(dated$correlation[1:4]))` and
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(dated$correlation[1:4]))` inside the episodes. The
caution of that chapter applies with more force here. A covariance matrix of
sixteen series has `r N * (N + 1) / 2` distinct entries, the liquidity shock
has `r dv("liquidity shock", "months")` months, and a correlation matrix from
`r dv("liquidity shock", "months")` observations has rank
`r dv("liquidity shock", "months") - 1L`; measured correlation also rises
mechanically with volatility [@forbes2002]. @tbl-19-dated describes; it cannot
be optimized on.

### A detected regime: the turbulence threshold

The index is the one of @sec-05-factor-models-application, from the same call.
Before thresholding it we check what a value is made of: the package returns a
monotone transform of @eq-05-turbulence, $\sqrt{d_t}/N$, computed from month
$t$ and the sixty months before it.

```{r}
#| label: turbulence
turb <- uncertaintymeasures::OSturbulence(R, rolling = TRUE, roll.obs = 60)$turb
tb   <- as.numeric(turb)
stopifnot(length(tb) == nrow(R), all(zoo::index(turb) == dates))

first_oos <- 121L                                    # the register's first out-of-sample month
past <- zoo::coredata(R)[(first_oos - 60L):(first_oos - 1L), ]
d    <- stats::mahalanobis(zoo::coredata(R)[first_oos, ], colMeans(past), stats::cov(past))
stopifnot(all.equal(tb[first_oos], sqrt(d) / N))
```

A month is flagged when the index exceeds the 75th percentile of its own
history, the convention of @kritzman2010, with the percentile computed on an
expanding window that ends the month before. The flag for month $t$ is known
at the end of month $t$ and decides the portfolio held in $t + 1$.

```{r}
#| label: turbulence-flag
turb_flag <- function(tb, q = 0.75, burn = 24L) {
  threshold <- vapply(seq_along(tb), function(t) {
    past <- tb[seq_len(t - 1L)]; past <- past[!is.na(past)]
    if (length(past) < burn) NA_real_ else stats::quantile(past, q, names = FALSE)
  }, numeric(1))
  tb > threshold
}
flag_turb <- turb_flag(tb)

# No look-ahead: reverse everything after `cut`, and the flags through `cut` must not move.
cut    <- first_oos + 119L
tb_alt <- replace(tb, (cut + 1L):length(tb), rev(tb[(cut + 1L):length(tb)]))
stopifnot(identical(turb_flag(tb_alt)[seq_len(cut)], flag_turb[seq_len(cut)]),
          !identical(turb_flag(tb_alt), flag_turb))
```

### A detected regime: a two-state hidden Markov model

@eq-19-model on all sixteen classes with two states has
`r 2 * N + N * (N + 1) + 2` parameters, two mean vectors, two covariance
matrices and two transition probabilities, against `r nrow(Re)` months. We fit
it instead to one summary series, the equal-weighted excess return of the
sixteen, where the same model has six. No hidden-Markov package is needed: the
filter of @eq-19-predict and @eq-19-update is a loop, the smoother of
@eq-19-smooth another, and EM alternates them with weighted moments.

```{r}
#| label: hmm
hamilton <- function(y, th) {
  n <- length(y); filt <- pred <- matrix(NA_real_, n, 2); loglik <- 0
  dens <- cbind(stats::dnorm(y, th$mu[1], th$sigma[1]), stats::dnorm(y, th$mu[2], th$sigma[2]))
  xi <- c(0.5, 0.5)                                  # prior for the first month
  for (t in seq_len(n)) {
    pred[t, ] <- xi                                  # xi_{t|t-1}
    joint     <- xi * dens[t, ]
    loglik    <- loglik + log(sum(joint))
    filt[t, ] <- joint / sum(joint)                  # the update step
    xi        <- as.numeric(filt[t, ] %*% th$P)      # the prediction step
  }
  list(filtered = filt, predicted = pred, loglik = loglik)
}

kim <- function(h, P) {                              # smoothed probabilities
  sm <- h$filtered
  for (t in (nrow(sm) - 1L):1L)
    sm[t, ] <- h$filtered[t, ] * as.numeric(P %*% (sm[t + 1L, ] / h$predicted[t + 1L, ]))
  sm
}

fit_hmm <- function(y, max_iter = 200L, tol = 1e-6) {
  far <- abs(y - stats::median(y)); hi <- far > stats::quantile(far, 0.8)
  th  <- list(mu = c(mean(y[!hi]), mean(y[hi])), sigma = c(stats::sd(y[!hi]), stats::sd(y[hi])),
              P = rbind(c(0.95, 0.05), c(0.10, 0.90)))
  floor_sd <- stats::sd(y) / 4; ll_old <- -Inf; n <- length(y)
  for (iter in seq_len(max_iter)) {
    h  <- hamilton(y, th); sm <- kim(h, th$P)                                # E-step
    J  <- (t(h$filtered[-n, ]) %*% (sm[-1L, ] / h$predicted[-1L, ])) * th$P  # expected transitions
    th$P     <- J / rowSums(J)                                               # M-step
    th$mu    <- colSums(sm * y) / colSums(sm)
    th$sigma <- pmax(sqrt(colSums(sm * outer(y, th$mu, "-")^2) / colSums(sm)), floor_sd)
    if (h$loglik - ll_old < tol) break
    ll_old <- h$loglik
  }
  o <- order(th$sigma)                               # state 2 is the high-volatility state
  list(mu = th$mu[o], sigma = th$sigma[o], P = th$P[o, o], loglik = h$loglik, iter = iter)
}

y        <- rowMeans(X)                              # equal-weighted excess return
fit_full <- fit_hmm(y)
smoothed <- kim(hamilton(y, fit_full), fit_full$P)[, 2]
round(c(mu = 12 * fit_full$mu, sigma = sqrt(12) * fit_full$sigma, stay = diag(fit_full$P)), 3)
```

The volatility floor is there because the likelihood of a Gaussian mixture is
unbounded when one state collapses onto a single observation. On the full
sample the two states differ in volatility,
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * sqrt(12) * fit_full$sigma[1])` against
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * sqrt(12) * fit_full$sigma[2])` a year, and hardly in
mean; the high-volatility state lasts
`r sprintf("%.0f", 1 / (1 - fit_full$P[2, 2]))` months on average and the other
`r sprintf("%.0f", 1 / (1 - fit_full$P[1, 1]))`.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked: the mixture moments of the summary series

```{r}
#| label: mixture-scalar
P_hat   <- fit_full$P
pi_bar  <- c(P_hat[2, 1], P_hat[1, 2]) / (P_hat[1, 2] + P_hat[2, 1])     # long-run state shares
stopifnot(all.equal(as.numeric(pi_bar %*% P_hat), pi_bar))
sg      <- 100 * fit_full$sigma                                          # percent a month
within  <- sum(pi_bar * sg^2)
between <- sum(pi_bar * (100 * fit_full$mu - sum(pi_bar * 100 * fit_full$mu))^2)
kurt    <- 3 * (sum(pi_bar * sg^4) / within^2 - 1)
sample  <- c(kurtosis = as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::kurtosis(y, method = "excess")),
             skewness = as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::skewness(y)))
c(mixture_vol = sqrt(within + between), sample_vol = 100 * stats::sd(y),
  mixture_kurtosis = kurt, sample)
```

With long-run shares $\bar{\boldsymbol{\pi}} = (`r sprintf("%.2f", pi_bar[1])`,
`r sprintf("%.2f", pi_bar[2])`)$ and regime volatilities of
$\sigma_1 = `r sprintf("%.2f", sg[1])`$ and
$\sigma_2 = `r sprintf("%.2f", sg[2])`$ percent a month, the scalar version of
@eq-19-mixture gives

$$
\bar{\sigma}^2
= \underbrace{`r sprintf("%.2f", pi_bar[1])` \times `r sprintf("%.2f", sg[1])`^2
  + `r sprintf("%.2f", pi_bar[2])` \times `r sprintf("%.2f", sg[2])`^2}_{\text{within}}
  + \underbrace{`r sprintf("%.4f", between)`}_{\text{between}}
= `r sprintf("%.2f", within + between)` ,
$$

a volatility of `r sprintf("%.2f", sqrt(within + between))` percent a month
against `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * stats::sd(y))` in the sample, and
@eq-19-kurtosis gives

$$
\bar{K} = 3\left(\frac{`r sprintf("%.2f", pi_bar[1])` \times `r sprintf("%.2f", sg[1])`^4
                       + `r sprintf("%.2f", pi_bar[2])` \times `r sprintf("%.2f", sg[2])`^4}
                      {`r sprintf("%.2f", within)`^2} - 1\right)
        = `r sprintf("%.2f", kurt)` .
$$

Two Gaussian regimes account for an excess kurtosis of
`r sprintf("%.1f", kurt)` of the `r sprintf("%.1f", sample[["kurtosis"]])` in
the sample. They account for none of its skewness of
`r sprintf("%.2f", sample[["skewness"]])`: the fitted regime means are almost
equal, so the between-regime term is
`r sprintf("%.3f%%", 100 * between / (within + between))` of the variance.
What this model has found is a volatility regime rather than a bear market.
:::

Those estimates used every month. In real time the parameters are re-estimated
each December on an expanding window, the filter is run with them through each
month of the following year, and nothing after month $t$ enters the
probability for $t$.

```{r}
#| label: hmm-realtime
hmm_realtime <- function(y, start) {
  refit <- seq(start, length(y), by = 12L)
  fits  <- lapply(refit, function(e) fit_hmm(y[seq_len(e)]))
  prob  <- t(vapply(start:length(y), function(t) {
    th <- fits[[max(which(refit <= t))]]             # the latest fit, on data through its own date
    xi <- hamilton(y[seq_len(t)], th)$filtered[t, ]
    c(filtered = xi[2], predicted = as.numeric(xi %*% th$P)[2])
  }, numeric(2)))
  list(refit = refit, fits = fits, month = start:length(y), prob = prob)
}
rt <- hmm_realtime(y, start = first_oos - 1L)

# No look-ahead: the same procedure on a truncated sample returns the same probabilities.
cut_h <- first_oos + 23L
stopifnot(all.equal(hmm_realtime(y[seq_len(cut_h)], first_oos - 1L)$prob,
                    rt$prob[rt$month <= cut_h, ]))
```

```{r}
#| label: detection
live     <- rt$month                                 # months in which both detectors exist
flag_hmm <- rep(NA, length(y)); flag_hmm[live] <- rt$prob[, "filtered"] > 0.5
detect <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(ep)), function(i) {
  m   <- intersect(which(in_episode(dates, ep$episode[i])), live)
  lag <- function(f) if (any(f[m])) which(f[m])[1] - 1L else NA_integer_
  tibble::tibble(episode = ep$label[i], months = length(m),
                 turb_lag = lag(flag_turb), turb_share = mean(flag_turb[m]),
                 hmm_lag  = lag(flag_hmm),  hmm_share  = mean(flag_hmm[m]),
                 smoothed_share = mean(smoothed[m] > 0.5))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
calm_live <- setdiff(live, which(in_any))
false_alarm <- c(turbulence = mean(flag_turb[calm_live]), hmm = mean(flag_hmm[calm_live]),
                 smoothed = mean(smoothed[calm_live] > 0.5))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-19-probabilities
#| fig-cap: "Probability of the high-volatility state of the equal-weighted return. The smoothed line uses the full sample and its parameters; the filtered line uses, at each month, only data through that month and parameters re-estimated each December. Ticks along the bottom are months flagged by the turbulence threshold; the shaded bands are the four dated episodes."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.5
prob_frame <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(date = dates, value = smoothed, kind = "smoothed, full sample"),
  tibble::tibble(date = dates[live], value = rt$prob[, "filtered"], kind = "filtered, real time"),
  tibble::tibble(date = dates[which(flag_turb)], value = -0.06, kind = "turbulence flag"))

ggplot2::ggplot(dplyr::filter(prob_frame, kind != "turbulence flag"),
                ggplot2::aes(date, value)) +
  ggplot2::geom_rect(data = ep, inherit.aes = FALSE,
                     ggplot2::aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
                     fill = tidyaa_colors[["rule"]], alpha = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(colour = kind), linewidth = 0.5) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = dplyr::filter(prob_frame, kind == "turbulence flag"),
                      shape = 124, size = 2, colour = tidyaa_colors[["ink"]]) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(`smoothed, full sample` = tidyaa_colors[["ink"]],
                                          `filtered, real time` = tidyaa_colors[["broken"]])) +
  scale_x_model() +
  ggplot2::labs(y = "probability of the high-volatility state")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-19-detection
#| tbl-cap: "Detection of the four dated episodes from the first month both detectors exist. The lag is the number of months from the episode's first such month to the first flag; the share is the fraction of its months flagged. The last column is the smoothed probability, which uses the full sample."
#| echo: false
detect |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(turb_lag, hmm_lag), ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), "never", as.character(.x))),
                dplyr::across(dplyr::ends_with("share"), ~ sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * .x))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrrr",
        col.names = c("", "months", "turbulence: lag", "flagged", "filtered HMM: lag", "flagged",
                      "smoothed: flagged"))
```

```{r}
#| label: detection-facts
#| include: false
at_cap  <- sum(vapply(rt$fits, function(f) f$iter, numeric(1)) >= 200)
before  <- live[live < min(which(in_episode(dates, "credit_crisis")))]
dt <- function(e, col) detect[[col]][detect$episode == e]
stopifnot(mean(flag_hmm[before]) > 5 * mean(smoothed[before] > 0.5) + 0.1)
```

@fig-19-probabilities and @tbl-19-detection are the chapter's argument in
small. With hindsight the model is clean: the smoothed probability is above
one half in `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * dt("credit crisis", "smoothed_share"))`
of the credit-crisis months and in
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * false_alarm[["smoothed"]])` of the months outside
any episode. In real time it is not. Before the credit crisis the sample
contains no high-volatility regime to learn from, so the second state is
fitted to whatever divides a calm sample: EM stops at its iteration limit in
`r at_cap` of the `r length(rt$fits)` refits, and the filtered probability is
above one half in `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(flag_hmm[before]))` of the
months before that crisis against
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(smoothed[before] > 0.5))` for the smoothed
one. A regime cannot be detected by a model that has not yet seen it. Once it
has, the filter recognizes the liquidity shock
`r dt("liquidity shock", "hmm_lag")` month after it begins and the rates shock
after `r dt("rates shock", "hmm_lag")`; the turbulence threshold, which needs
no stress history, flags the credit crisis in its first month and the other
two after `r dt("liquidity shock", "turb_lag")` and
`r dt("rates shock", "turb_lag")`. Neither sees the equity bear market as a
whole, a slow decline with bonds rising that is unusual in direction and not in
size. Outside the episodes the threshold flags
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * false_alarm[["turbulence"]])` of months and the
filter `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * false_alarm[["hmm"]])`.

### Regime portfolios in `PortfolioAnalytics`

`PortfolioAnalytics` ships the machinery for the switching rule.
`combine.portfolios()` turns a list of specifications into one
`portfolio.list` object; `regime.portfolios()` attaches a regime series to
such a list; and `optimize.portfolio.rebalancing()` then solves, at each
rebalancing date, the specification the regime selects. Our two
specifications are a calm portfolio, the long-only tangency of @eq-09-tangency,
and a stress portfolio, long-only minimum variance.

```{r}
#| label: specs
#| warning: false
win <- 60L
base_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")
calm_spec   <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "StdDev")
stress_spec <- base_spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "StdDev")

both <- combine.portfolios(list(calm_spec, stress_spec))
opt_both <- optimize.portfolio(Re[(first_oos - win):(first_oos - 1L), ], both,
                               optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE)
w_both <- extractWeights(opt_both)
class(opt_both)
round(w_both[, colSums(w_both) > 0.02], 3)
```

Handed to `optimize.portfolio()` directly, a `portfolio.list` is solved
specification by specification and `extractWeights()` returns a matrix with a
row for each. The backtest needs both portfolios at every month. The stress
portfolio comes from `optimize.portfolio.rebalancing()` on a sixty-month
window, set up as in @sec-25-backtesting-implementation. The calm one is
computed as the single quadratic program of
@sec-08-estimation-error-implementation, because `maxSR = TRUE` under `ROI` is
a one-dimensional search that solves a quadratic program at every step, and
the package run below confirms that the two routes agree.

```{r}
#| label: two-portfolios
#| warning: false
reb <- (first_oos - 1L):(nrow(Re) - 1L)     # weights are set at the end of these months
oos <- reb + 1L                             # and earn the returns of these

# Long-only tangency: min y'Sy subject to y'mu = 1, y >= 0, then w = y / sum(y).
tan_qp <- function(mu, S) {
  n <- length(mu)
  if (max(mu) <= 0) return(setNames(rep(NA_real_, n), names(mu)))
  sol <- quadprog::solve.QP(Dmat = 2 * S * 1e4, dvec = rep(0, n),
                            Amat = cbind(mu * 1e2, diag(n)), bvec = c(1, rep(0, n)), meq = 1)
  y <- pmax(sol$solution, 0)
  setNames(y / sum(y), names(mu))
}
W_calm <- t(vapply(reb, function(t) {
  Z <- X[(t - win + 1L):t, ]; tan_qp(colMeans(Z), stats::cov(Z))
}, numeric(N)))

bt_stress <- optimize.portfolio.rebalancing(
  Re[(first_oos - win):nrow(Re), ], stress_spec, optimize_method = "ROI",
  rebalance_on = "months", training_period = win, rolling_window = win - 1L)
W_stress <- extractWeights(bt_stress)
W_stress <- zoo::coredata(W_stress)[match(dates[reb], zoo::index(W_stress)), colnames(Re)]

dimnames(W_calm) <- list(as.character(dates[reb]), colnames(Re))
rownames(W_stress) <- rownames(W_calm)
stopifnot(!anyNA(W_calm), !anyNA(W_stress))
```

The regime object is built from the turbulence flags, coded 1 for calm and 2
for stress, and run over a short stretch that begins with the credit crisis.

```{r}
#| label: regime-run
#| warning: false
regime_turb <- xts::xts(ifelse(flag_turb, 2L, 1L), order.by = dates)[!is.na(flag_turb)]
reg_spec    <- regime.portfolios(regime_turb, both)

demo <- min(which(in_episode(dates, "credit_crisis"))) + 0:17
bt_demo <- optimize.portfolio.rebalancing(
  Re[(demo[1] - win + 1L):max(demo), ], reg_spec, optimize_method = "ROI",
  rebalance_on = "months", training_period = win, rolling_window = win - 1L, maxSR = TRUE)
W_demo <- extractWeights(bt_demo)
used   <- vapply(bt_demo$opt_rebalancing, function(o) o$regime, numeric(1))

by_hand <- W_calm[as.character(dates[demo]), ]
by_hand[used == 2, ] <- W_stress[as.character(dates[demo]), ][used == 2, ]
stopifnot(all(zoo::index(W_demo) == dates[demo]),
          all(used == as.numeric(regime_turb[dates[demo]])),   # the regime of the rebalancing date itself
          used[1] == 2,
          max(abs(zoo::coredata(W_demo) - by_hand)) < 1e-6)
table(specification = used)
```

The assertions say what the package did: at every date it read the regime of
that date, solved the matching specification on the trailing window, and
returned the weights we obtain by picking rows from the two separate runs.
Switching in the package is row selection. What it does around that is worth
measuring before it is trusted.

```{r}
#| label: quirks
#| warning: false
pick <- function(regime, t, specs = both) {     # the specification a regime series selects at month t
  o <- try(optimize.portfolio(Re[(t - win + 1L):t, ], regime.portfolios(regime, specs),
                              optimize_method = "ROI"), silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(o, "try-error")) NULL else o
}
t_stress <- demo[1]; t_calm <- max(which(!flag_turb[seq_len(demo[1])]))
shifted  <- xts::xts(zoo::coredata(regime_turb), order.by = zoo::index(regime_turb) + 1)
half     <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "weight_sum", min_sum = 0.5, max_sum = 0.5) |>
  add.constraint(type = "box", min = 0, max = 0.2) |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "StdDev")

quirk <- list(
  coded_01_stress = pick(regime_turb - 1L, t_stress)$regime,     # 1: the calm specification
  coded_01_calm   = is.null(pick(regime_turb - 1L, t_calm)),     # TRUE: index zero, the solve fails
  dates_shifted   = pick(shifted, t_stress)$regime,              # 1, with a warning
  third_value     = inherits(try(regime.portfolios(replace(regime_turb, 1, 3L), both),
                                 silent = TRUE), "try-error"),
  half_invested   = sum(extractWeights(pick(regime_turb, t_stress,
                                            combine.portfolios(list(calm_spec, half))))),
  stats_labels    = lengths(extractStats(bt_demo)),
  measure_labels  = vapply(extractObjectiveMeasures(bt_demo), nrow, integer(1)))
stopifnot(identical(quirk$coded_01_stress, 1), quirk$coded_01_calm,
          identical(quirk$dates_shifted, 1), as.numeric(regime_turb[dates[t_stress]]) == 2,
          quirk$third_value, abs(quirk$half_invested - 0.5) < 1e-8,
          quirk$stats_labels[["regime.1"]] == sum(used == 2),
          quirk$measure_labels[["regime.1"]] == sum(used == 1))
str(quirk, give.attr = FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What `regime.portfolios()` does with the regime series

Each line is one of the measurements above.

- **The regime is a list index.** `optimize.portfolio()` selects
  `portfolio.list[[regime]]`, so the series must be coded 1, 2, … in the order
  of the list. A series coded 0 and 1 passes the constructor. A stress month,
  coded 1, then receives the calm specification without a message, and a calm
  month, coded 0, fails and leaves a row of `NA` in the weights.
- **The lookup is contemporaneous.** The regime is read at the last date of
  the estimation window, the rebalancing date. The series must hold at each
  date what was known on that date; a hand-dated series is used unlagged, and
  a regime dated with hindsight enters the backtest with nothing to mark it.
- **Dates must match exactly.** When the rebalancing date is missing from the
  regime index, here because the index is a day off, the first specification
  is used and the only trace is a warning.
- **Every value needs a specification and every specification a value.** The
  constructor counts distinct values and refuses a series with a third value,
  with an `NA`, or one that never visits a regime.
- **Only the assets must agree.** Constraints and objectives may differ: a
  stress specification confined to half the budget, with the rest in the
  bill, returns weights that sum to `r sprintf("%.1f", quirk$half_invested)`.
- **Arguments in `...` reach every specification.** `maxSR = TRUE` is passed
  to the stress specification too, which has no return objective; its weights
  are unaffected and a warning is raised at each stress date.
- **`extractWeights()` returns one `xts`**, a row per rebalancing date,
  whichever specification produced it, and the regime used is in
  `$opt_rebalancing[[i]]$regime`. `extractObjectiveMeasures()` and
  `extractStats()` return lists by regime and label them differently: the
  first sorts the regimes, the second numbers them in order of first
  appearance, so that here its `regime.1` holds the
  `r quirk$stats_labels[["regime.1"]]` stress dates.
:::

## Detected Against Dated Regimes, Out of Sample {#sec-19-regimes-application}

### The strategies and their accounting

From observation `r first_oos`, the first month of model year
`r model_year(dates[first_oos])` and the start of the register of
@sec-25-backtesting-application, we run the static policy, which holds the
calm portfolio throughout, and four alternatives; the stress portfolio held
throughout is reported beside them as a second static row. Three switch to the stress
portfolio by @eq-19-switch: on the dated episodes, using the label of the
month the return is earned in, which no investor had and which is the
infeasible upper bound; on the turbulence flag of the rebalancing month; and
on the predicted probability of @eq-19-predict from the real-time filter. The
fourth holds the tangency portfolio of the mixture moments of @eq-19-mixture.
For it the regime moments of the sixteen classes are sample moments weighted
by the smoothed probabilities of each December's fit, on the expanding sample
because a sixty-month window need not contain a stress month at all.

```{r}
#| label: strategies
#| warning: false
p_stress <- rep(NA_real_, length(y)); p_stress[rt$month] <- rt$prob[, "predicted"]
stress_by <- list(dated      = in_any[oos],          # the month ahead: hindsight
                  turbulence = flag_turb[reb],       # known at the rebalancing date
                  hmm        = p_stress[reb] > 0.5)
stopifnot(!anyNA(unlist(stress_by)))
switch_W <- function(s) { W <- W_calm; W[s, ] <- W_stress[s, ]; W }

regime_moments <- function(k) {                      # weighted moments of the sixteen at refit k
  e  <- rt$refit[k]; th <- rt$fits[[k]]
  sm <- kim(hamilton(y[seq_len(e)], th), th$P)
  list(m = lapply(1:2, function(s) stats::cov.wt(X[seq_len(e), ], wt = sm[, s] / sum(sm[, s]),
                                                 method = "ML")),
       share = colMeans(sm), n_eff = colSums(sm),
       all = stats::cov.wt(X[seq_len(e), ], method = "ML"))
}
mixture <- function(m, p) {                          # the mixture moments
  mu <- p[1] * m[[1]]$center + p[2] * m[[2]]$center
  S  <- p[1] * (m[[1]]$cov + tcrossprod(m[[1]]$center - mu)) +
        p[2] * (m[[2]]$cov + tcrossprod(m[[2]]$center - mu))
  list(mu = mu, S = S)
}
rm_k <- lapply(seq_along(rt$refit), regime_moments)

# At the sample's own state shares the mixture is the sample: the law of total covariance.
chk <- mixture(rm_k[[1]]$m, rm_k[[1]]$share)
stopifnot(all.equal(chk$mu, rm_k[[1]]$all$center), all.equal(chk$S, rm_k[[1]]$all$cov))

mix_at <- function(t) mixture(rm_k[[max(which(rt$refit <= t))]]$m, c(1 - p_stress[t], p_stress[t]))
W_mix  <- t(vapply(reb, function(t) { m <- mix_at(t); tan_qp(m$mu, m$S) }, numeric(N)))
dimnames(W_mix) <- dimnames(W_calm)
stopifnot(!anyNA(W_mix))

# The same portfolio from the package, with the mixture moments supplied through momentFUN.
make_moments <- function(mu, S) {
  force(mu); force(S)
  function(R, portfolio, ...) list(mu = mu, sigma = S, m3 = NULL, m4 = NULL, mean = mu, var = S)
}
m1    <- mix_at(reb[1])
w_pkg <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re, calm_spec, optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE,
                                           momentFUN = make_moments(m1$mu, m1$S)))
stopifnot(max(abs(w_pkg[colnames(Re)] - W_mix[1, ])) < 1e-4)
```

The accounting is that of the register: weights set at the end of month $t$
earn the returns of $t + 1$, drift, and are traded back at the turnover of
@eq-23-turnover and the cost of @eq-23-net, at the per-class rates of
`pm_costs_default()` from @sec-23-rebalancing-application. A switch is a
trade like any other, so its cost is in the same column.

```{r}
#| label: accounting
cost_rate <- pm_costs_default()[sub(".*_", "", colnames(R))]
stopifnot(!anyNA(cost_rate)); names(cost_rate) <- colnames(R)

run_path <- function(W) {
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(W), colnames(R)), nrow(W) == length(oos))
  Rm    <- zoo::coredata(R)[oos, ]
  gross <- rowSums(W * Rm)                                       # month t+1, weights set at t
  held  <- rbind(0, (W * (1 + Rm) / (1 + gross))[-nrow(W), ])    # drifted weights; flat before the first trade
  trade <- abs(W - held)
  tibble::tibble(date = dates[oos], gross = gross, turnover = rowSums(trade) / 2,
                 cost = as.numeric(trade %*% cost_rate)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(net = gross - cost)
}
sharpe_of <- function(r) {                                       # as the register: compounded, over the bill
  n <- length(r)
  (prod(1 + r)^(12 / n) - prod(1 + rf[oos])^(12 / n)) / (stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12))
}
performance <- function(path) {
  x <- xts::xts(path$gross, order.by = path$date)
  tibble::tibble(vol = stats::sd(path$gross) * sqrt(12), sharpe = sharpe_of(path$gross),
                 es = as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::ES(x, p = 0.95, method = "historical",
                                                          invert = FALSE)),
                 drawdown = as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::maxDrawdown(x)),
                 turnover = 12 * mean(path$turnover), cost = 12 * mean(path$cost),
                 sharpe_net = sharpe_of(path$net))
}
# Difference of two Sharpe ratios in standard errors (Jobson-Korkie, as corrected by Memmel).
z_against <- function(p, q) {
  a <- p$gross - rf[oos]; b <- q$gross - rf[oos]
  s <- c(mean(a) / stats::sd(a), mean(b) / stats::sd(b)); rho <- stats::cor(a, b)
  (s[1] - s[2]) / sqrt((2 - 2 * rho + (s[1]^2 + s[2]^2 - 2 * s[1] * s[2] * rho^2) / 2) / length(a))
}

label <- c(static = "static: calm portfolio", stress = "static: stress portfolio",
           dated = "switching, dated (infeasible)", turbulence = "switching, turbulence",
           hmm = "switching, filtered HMM", mixture = "mixture mean-variance")
weights <- c(list(static = W_calm, stress = W_stress), lapply(stress_by, switch_W),
             list(mixture = W_mix))
stopifnot(identical(names(weights), names(label)))
paths <- lapply(weights, run_path)
share <- c(static = 0, stress = 1, vapply(stress_by, mean, numeric(1)), mixture = NA)

perf <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(paths, performance), .id = "key") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    z = vapply(paths, z_against, numeric(1), q = paths$static),
    stress_share = share[key],
    same_mix = vapply(stress_share, function(s) {    # the constant mix with the same time in stress
      if (is.na(s)) NA_real_ else sharpe_of(run_path(s * W_stress + (1 - s) * W_calm)$gross)
    }, numeric(1)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-19-cumulative
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative return of the six strategies, gross of costs, from the first out-of-sample month. The shaded bands are the dated episodes."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.55
cum <- lapply(names(paths), function(k) {
  tibble::tibble(date = paths[[k]]$date, value = cumprod(1 + paths[[k]]$gross) - 1, kind = label[[k]])
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  dplyr::mutate(kind = factor(kind, levels = unname(label)))

ggplot2::ggplot(cum, ggplot2::aes(date, value)) +
  ggplot2::geom_rect(data = dplyr::mutate(ep, start = pmax(start, min(cum$date))),
                     inherit.aes = FALSE,
                     ggplot2::aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
                     fill = tidyaa_colors[["rule"]], alpha = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(colour = kind), linewidth = 0.55) +
  scale_colour_tidyaa() +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_x_model() +
  ggplot2::labs(y = "cumulative return")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-19-performance
#| tbl-cap: "Six strategies on the sixteen classes, monthly, over the register's out-of-sample months. Volatility, Sharpe ratio, historical 95% expected shortfall and maximum drawdown are gross of costs; z is the difference from the static policy's Sharpe ratio in standard errors; cost is the annual return lost to trading; the last two columns give the share of months in the stress portfolio and the Sharpe ratio of the constant mix of the two portfolios with that share."
#| echo: false
fmt_pct <- function(x, d = 1) ifelse(is.na(x), "", sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * x))
perf |>
  dplyr::transmute(strategy = label[key], vol = fmt_pct(vol), sharpe = sprintf("%.3f", sharpe),
                   z = ifelse(key == "static", "", sprintf("%+.2f", z)),
                   es = fmt_pct(es), drawdown = fmt_pct(drawdown), turnover = fmt_pct(turnover, 0),
                   cost = sprintf("%.0f bp", 1e4 * cost), sharpe_net = sprintf("%.3f", sharpe_net),
                   stress_share = fmt_pct(stress_share, 0),
                   same_mix = ifelse(is.na(same_mix), "", sprintf("%.3f", same_mix))) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrrrrrrr",
        col.names = c("", "volatility", "Sharpe", "z", "ES 95%", "max drawdown", "turnover", "cost",
                      "Sharpe, net", "in stress", "same mix"))
```

```{r}
#| label: performance-facts
#| include: false
register <- utils::read.csv("output/tables/oos-sweep.csv") |>
  dplyr::filter(universe == "classes", window == win, frequency == "months", basis == "gross")
reg_sr <- function(s) register$sharpe[match(s, register$strategy)]
pv <- function(k, col) perf[[col]][perf$key == k]
se_static <- sqrt((1 + (pv("static", "sharpe") / sqrt(12))^2 / 2) / length(oos)) * sqrt(12)
advantage <- pv("dated", "sharpe") - pv("static", "sharpe")
kept      <- function(k) (pv(k, "sharpe") - pv("static", "sharpe")) / advantage
timing    <- function(k) pv(k, "sharpe") - pv(k, "same_mix")
detected  <- c("turbulence", "hmm")
pre_cc    <- oos < min(which(in_episode(dates, "credit_crisis")))
hmm_pre   <- mean(stress_by$hmm[pre_cc]); hmm_post <- mean(stress_by$hmm[!pre_cc])
stopifnot(pv("hmm", "sharpe") < pv("static", "sharpe"), pv("turbulence", "sharpe") > pv("static", "sharpe"),
          abs(pv("static", "sharpe") - reg_sr("max_sharpe")) < 0.005,
          abs(pv("stress", "sharpe") - reg_sr("min_variance")) < 0.005,
          advantage > 0, timing("dated") > 0,
          all(vapply(detected, function(k) pv("stress", "sharpe") > pv(k, "sharpe"), logical(1))),
          all(abs(perf$z[perf$key %in% detected]) < 1.96),
          timing("turbulence") < timing("dated"), timing("hmm") < timing("dated"))
```

### Reading the result

The two static rows are checks before they are results. The static policy's
Sharpe ratio of `r sprintf("%.3f", pv("static", "sharpe"))` is the register's
`r sprintf("%.3f", reg_sr("max_sharpe"))` for the maximum-Sharpe strategy at
this window, and the stress portfolio's
`r sprintf("%.3f", pv("stress", "sharpe"))` is its
`r sprintf("%.3f", reg_sr("min_variance"))` for minimum variance, both read
from `output/tables/oos-sweep.csv`; the accounting here is the register's.

With the regimes dated, switching works. The infeasible strategy raises the
Sharpe ratio from `r sprintf("%.3f", pv("static", "sharpe"))` to
`r sprintf("%.3f", pv("dated", "sharpe"))` and cuts the maximum drawdown from
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * pv("static", "drawdown"))` to
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * pv("dated", "drawdown"))` while spending
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * pv("dated", "stress_share"))` of the months in the
stress portfolio. The constant mix with the same share earns
`r sprintf("%.3f", pv("dated", "same_mix"))`, so
`r sprintf("%.2f", timing("dated"))` of the gain is timing and the rest is
holding some of a portfolio that the register already ranks above the calm
one.

That last column is what the detected strategies have to be read against. The
turbulence switch reaches `r sprintf("%.3f", pv("turbulence", "sharpe"))`,
which keeps `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * kept("turbulence"))` of the dated
strategy's advantage over the static policy, and it is
`r sprintf("%+.2f", timing("turbulence"))` against its own constant mix: the
flag chooses its months no better than a fixed blend would, at
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * pv("turbulence", "turnover"))` turnover and
`r sprintf("%.0f", 1e4 * pv("turbulence", "cost"))` basis points a year in
costs against `r sprintf("%.0f", 1e4 * pv("static", "cost"))` for the static
policy. The filtered model reaches
`r sprintf("%.3f", pv("hmm", "sharpe"))`, below the static policy, and it is
in the stress portfolio in `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * pv("hmm", "stress_share"))`
of all months against `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * pv("dated", "stress_share"))`
for the dated regimes: in `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * hmm_pre)` of the months
before the credit crisis, where the smoothed probability of
@fig-19-probabilities marks almost nothing, and in
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * hmm_post)` of the months from the crisis on, most
of them the model years of elevated volatility that follow it. The constant
mix with its share earns `r sprintf("%.3f", pv("hmm", "same_mix"))`, so its
timing is worth `r sprintf("%+.2f", timing("hmm"))`, against
`r sprintf("%+.2f", timing("dated"))` for the dated regimes. The mixture rule,
at `r sprintf("%.3f", pv("mixture", "sharpe"))`, is
`r if (pv("mixture", "sharpe") < pv("static", "sharpe")) "below" else "above"`
the static policy: its regime covariance matrices are estimated from as few
as `r sprintf("%.0f", min(vapply(rm_k, function(r) min(r$n_eff), numeric(1))))`
effective months, and @eq-19-mixture passes that error to the optimizer.

None of this is distinguishable from sampling error. By @eq-25-se the
standard error of the static policy's Sharpe ratio over `r length(oos)` months
is `r sprintf("%.2f", se_static)`; the paired statistic in the z column, which
uses the correlation between the two return series [@memmel2003], is
`r sprintf("%+.2f", pv("turbulence", "z"))` for the turbulence switch and
`r sprintf("%+.2f", pv("hmm", "z"))` for the filtered model, and
`r sprintf("%+.2f", pv("dated", "z"))` for the strategy that knew the dates.
And one row needs no detector at all: the stress portfolio held throughout has
a Sharpe ratio of `r sprintf("%.3f", pv("stress", "sharpe"))`, above both
detected strategies. On this market the question of when to hold the
minimum-variance portfolio matters less than the question of whether to.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-19-episodes
#| tbl-cap: "Cumulative gross return of each strategy inside each dated episode, over the episode's out-of-sample months."
#| echo: false
episode_ret <- lapply(names(paths), function(k) {
  tibble::tibble(key = k, episode = ep$label,
                 months = vapply(ep$episode, function(e) sum(in_episode(paths[[k]]$date, e)), integer(1)),
                 ret = vapply(ep$episode, function(e)
                   prod(1 + paths[[k]]$gross[in_episode(paths[[k]]$date, e)]) - 1, numeric(1)))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()

episode_tab <- episode_ret |>
  dplyr::mutate(strategy = label[key], episode = sprintf("%s (%d months)", episode, months),
                ret = sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * ret)) |>
  dplyr::select(strategy, episode, ret) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = episode, values_from = ret)
kable(episode_tab, align = "lrrrr", col.names = c("", names(episode_tab)[-1]))
```

```{r}
#| label: episode-facts
#| include: false
er <- function(k, e) episode_ret$ret[episode_ret$key == k & episode_ret$episode == e]
cc_oos    <- in_episode(dates[oos], "credit_crisis")
enter_hmm <- which(stress_by$hmm[cc_oos])[1]                 # first crisis month held in the stress portfolio
lost_first <- prod(1 + paths$static$gross[cc_oos][seq_len(enter_hmm - 1L)]) - 1
stopifnot(enter_hmm == dt("credit crisis", "hmm_lag") + 2L, lost_first < 0,
          er("stress", "credit crisis") > er("static", "credit crisis"),
          er("stress", "rates shock") < 0, er("dated", "rates shock") < 0,
          all(vapply(detected, function(k) er(k, "rates shock") < er("stress", "rates shock"), logical(1))))
```

@tbl-19-episodes shows where each number comes from. In the credit crisis the
static policy loses `r sprintf("%.1f%%", -100 * er("static", "credit crisis"))`
and the stress portfolio
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", -100 * er("stress", "credit crisis"))`. The turbulence
switch, flagged in the first month, captures most of the difference at
`r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * er("turbulence", "credit crisis"))`. The filtered
model, at `r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * er("hmm", "credit crisis"))`, captures
almost none of it: it flags the crisis one month after it begins, the switch
takes effect the month after that, and by then the static policy had already
lost `r sprintf("%.1f%%", -100 * lost_first)`, against
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", -100 * er("static", "credit crisis"))` for the episode
as a whole.
That is the episode a two-state model is built for, and a lag of two months
was enough to miss it. In the rates shock there
is nothing to capture: the stress portfolio is mostly government bonds, it
loses `r sprintf("%.1f%%", -100 * er("stress", "rates shock"))`, and the
investor who knew every date loses the same. The detected strategies lose
more, `r sprintf("%.1f%%", -100 * er("turbulence", "rates shock"))` and
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", -100 * er("hmm", "rates shock"))`, because they enter and
leave during it. A stress portfolio is a hedge against the stress that
resembles the past, and @tbl-19-dated had already said that the fourth episode
does not.

Three limits on that conclusion. One path of `r length(oos)` months contains
`r sum(episode_ret$months[episode_ret$key == "static"] > 0)` episodes, and the
ranking of the detectors rests on them. The threshold, the summary series,
the number of states and the two portfolios were each chosen once and not
searched over, which is why the exercises vary them rather than the chapter.
And the stress portfolio is a model too: what to do when the regime model
itself may be wrong, rather than only its state, is the question of
@sec-28-robustness-theory.

## Key Takeaways {.unnumbered}

- A regime-switching model is @eq-19-model plus a filter. The prediction and
  update steps of @eq-19-predict and @eq-19-update give the probability of
  each state from data through $t$; the smoother of @eq-19-smooth gives it
  from the whole sample, and only the first is available to an investor
  [@hamilton1989; @kim1994].
- One month ahead the investor faces the mixture moments of @eq-19-mixture.
  The covariance contains a between-regime term, and a mixture of Gaussian
  regimes has fat tails by @eq-19-kurtosis; the two-state model of the
  equal-weighted return accounts for about half of its excess kurtosis and
  none of its skewness.
- Dating and detecting are different operations. Smoothed probabilities and
  full-sample parameters both carry the future into a backtest, and before the
  first stress regime has occurred a two-state model has nothing to detect it
  with.
- `regime.portfolios()` switches between specifications by a regime series
  and is equivalent to selecting rows from separate rebalancing runs. It reads
  the regime of the rebalancing date itself, uses the regime value as a list
  index, and checks neither the coding nor the timing of the series.
- On this market the infeasible dated switch is well ahead of the static
  policy; the turbulence switch keeps a small part of that by point estimate,
  the filtered model none, neither is distinguishable from the static policy
  by a paired test, and holding the stress portfolio throughout has a higher
  Sharpe ratio than either detector. In the rates shock no version of
  the switch helps, because the stress portfolio was built for a different
  stress.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. The turbulence flag uses the 75th percentile. Recompute the switching
   strategy with the 50th and the 90th, and report for each the share of
   months in the stress portfolio, the Sharpe ratio, and the Sharpe ratio of
   the constant mix with the same share. Which threshold, if any, times its
   months?
2. `regime.portfolios()` reads the regime of the rebalancing date. Feed the
   dated episodes to the switch in that way, so that the portfolio for month
   $t + 1$ is chosen by the label of month $t$, and compare with the
   infeasible row of @tbl-19-performance. How much of the dated advantage is
   lost to a delay of one month, and in which episode?
3. Simulate 100,000 months from a two-state chain with annual regime
   volatilities of 6% and 14%, equal means, and probabilities of staying of
   0.98 and 0.93. Compare the sample excess kurtosis with @eq-19-kurtosis, and
   compute the first-order autocorrelation of the squared returns. Which
   property of @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application does the persistence
   of the chain add to the fat tails?
4. Replace the stress portfolio by one that puts half the budget in the bill:
   half of the minimum-variance weights, which in `PortfolioAnalytics` is a
   `weight_sum` constraint of 0.5. Recompute the dated switch and its return
   inside each episode. Does leaving the market help in the rates shock where
   moving to bonds did not?
